Beginner Glossary — Words You'll See Everywhere

Plain-English definitions before we dive in

🎓
New to this? Read this glossary first. Every term here will appear throughout the guide. You don't need to memorize it — just refer back when something is unclear.
Jetson
A small, credit-card-to-book-sized computer made by NVIDIA. It has a powerful GPU (graphics chip) built in, designed specifically to run AI models. Think of it as a specialized mini-PC that excels at video analysis. The "Orin Nano Super" is one specific model.
JetPack
The "operating system bundle" for Jetson. Like Windows is for a regular PC, JetPack is the OS + all the GPU drivers + tools that come pre-installed. You flash this onto your Jetson's storage when you first set it up. Version 6.1 is what we use.
CUDA
A software layer that lets programs talk to the GPU. When a program says "I need GPU acceleration," it goes through CUDA. You don't code CUDA yourself — it runs in the background. Version 12.6 comes with JetPack 6.1.
TensorRT
NVIDIA's tool that takes an AI model (like YOLO) and compresses/optimizes it specifically for the Jetson's GPU. The first time you run inference, TensorRT "compiles" the model into a .engine file. This takes 5–15 minutes but only happens once — after that, startup is fast.
YOLO
"You Only Look Once" — a popular AI model for detecting objects in video frames. It draws bounding boxes around objects (person, car, etc.) in real time. YOLO26 refers to using the export script designed for DeepStream compatibility.
ONNX
A universal file format for AI models. We convert the YOLO .pt (PyTorch) file into .onnx format so that TensorRT can read and optimize it. Think of it like converting a .docx file to .pdf so a different app can open it.
DeepStream
NVIDIA's video analytics framework. It handles taking video (from files, cameras, or RTSP streams), feeding frames to the AI model, drawing detection boxes on the output, and sending the result somewhere (screen, file, RTSP stream). Think of it as the "plumbing" that connects the camera to YOLO to the display.
RTSP
"Real-Time Streaming Protocol." This is how IP cameras send video over a network. A CCTV camera has an RTSP URL like rtsp://192.168.1.100:554/stream. DeepStream can receive these streams as input AND can output its annotated video as an RTSP stream too.
GStreamer
The underlying video pipeline framework. DeepStream is built on top of GStreamer. You don't usually interact with it directly, but error messages often mention it (GST_DEBUG). It handles decoding/encoding video efficiently.
FP32 / FP16
Precision formats for numbers in AI computations. FP32 = 32-bit (full precision, slower). FP16 = 16-bit (half precision, ~2× faster, almost identical accuracy). Always use FP16 on Jetson — it has special hardware for it.
Batch Size
How many video frames the GPU processes at once. If you have 4 cameras, set batch-size=4 so the GPU processes one frame from each camera simultaneously. This is much more efficient than processing them one by one.
config file (.txt)
A plain text file with settings. DeepStream reads two config files: one for the AI model (config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt) and one for the overall pipeline (deepstream_app_config.txt). You edit these files to change behavior — no programming required.
Streammux
Short for "Stream Multiplexer." It takes multiple incoming video streams and combines them into one batch for the AI model to process. Like a traffic merge lane — multiple streams come in, one batched stream goes to inference.
Tiled Display
Showing multiple camera streams in a grid on one screen. Like a security monitoring room with 4 screens on one TV. DeepStream can do this natively with its tiled-display feature.

What is YOLO26? Understanding the Full Stack

How all the pieces connect together

What "YOLO26" Actually Means

"YOLO26" is not a version number like YOLO v1, v8, v11. Instead, it refers to the export script in the DeepStream-Yolo repository called export_yolo26.py. This script was written specifically to export YOLO models (any version — v8, v11, etc.) into the exact ONNX format that DeepStream expects.

ℹ️
In plain English: You have a YOLO model file (like yolo11s.pt). The "26" export script converts it into a format DeepStream can use. When we say "YOLO26 setup" we mean "using the export_yolo26.py script from the DeepStream-Yolo repo."

The Complete Software Stack

Here's what every piece does and why it's needed:

1

YOLO Model (.pt file)

The AI brain — a pre-trained neural network that knows how to detect 80 object types (person, car, bicycle, etc.). Downloaded as a .pt (PyTorch) file from Ultralytics. The "s" in yolo11s means "small" — best for Jetson Orin Nano Super.

2

export_yolo26.py → ONNX file

This script converts the .pt model into .onnx format. ONNX is a universal model format that TensorRT can understand. The conversion also restructures the model's output layers to match what DeepStream's parser expects.

3

TensorRT → .engine file

On first run, DeepStream calls TensorRT to compile the .onnx into a .engine file optimized specifically for YOUR Jetson's GPU. This takes 5-15 minutes but only once.

4

nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo.so

A compiled C++ library (plugin) that teaches DeepStream how to read YOLO's output boxes. Without this, DeepStream wouldn't understand the bounding box format that YOLO produces.

5

DeepStream Pipeline

Orchestrates everything: pulls video from cameras → decodes → feeds to AI → draws boxes on detected objects → sends to output (screen/RTSP/file).

4

Key Design Principles

🔄 Edge Jetsons = Processors

  • Each edge Jetson handles its zone's cameras
  • Runs YOLO inference locally
  • Outputs annotated RTSP stream
  • Reduces bandwidth (sends processed video, not raw)

🎯 Master Jetson = Aggregator

  • Receives RTSP streams from all edge Jetsons
  • Optionally runs secondary AI (counting, alerts)
  • Shows tiled view of all streams on one screen
  • Can re-stream to remote monitoring software

First-Time Jetson Boot Setup (Very Detailed)

Complete guide for someone turning on their Jetson for the very first time

🎓
Absolute beginner note: If this is your first time, the Jetson Orin Nano Super comes as a Developer Kit. You need: the Jetson board + power adapter + microSD card (64GB+ recommended) OR NVMe SSD + a monitor + keyboard + mouse + ethernet cable or WiFi.

What You Need Before Starting

ItemPurposeNotes
Jetson Orin Nano Super Dev KitThe main computerComes with board + module
microSD card (64GB+) or NVMe SSDStorage for OS and filesNVMe is faster, recommended
Power adapter (19V DC barrel)PowerComes in the kit box
HDMI monitor + cableFirst-time display setupCan go headless later
USB keyboard + mouseFirst-time setup inputCan use SSH later
Ethernet cable + routerNetwork connectionFor downloading packages
Host PC (Ubuntu 22.04)To flash JetPack (optional)Only needed for SDK Manager method

Method 1 — Flash with SD Card Image (Easiest)

This is the recommended method for beginners. You download an image and write it directly to the SD card.

1

Download Jetson Orin Nano Super SD Card Image

Go to developer.nvidia.com/embedded/downloads → Find "Jetson Orin Nano Developer Kit" → Download JetPack 6.1 SD Card image (.img.gz file, ~12GB)

2

Flash the SD card using Balena Etcher

Download Balena Etcher (free, at etcher.balena.io). Open it → Select the .img.gz file → Select your SD card → Click Flash. Takes about 15 minutes.

3

Insert SD card and power on

Insert the flashed SD card into the Jetson's SD slot. Connect monitor, keyboard, mouse, ethernet. Plug in power. The Jetson boots into Ubuntu setup.

4

Complete Ubuntu initial setup

Follow the on-screen prompts: pick language → create username and password → accept license. The username/password you create here is what you'll use for SSH and the terminal.

After First Boot — Essential Commands

⚠️
Run these EVERY TIME before doing any AI work. They set the Jetson to maximum performance mode. Without this, you'll get much lower FPS.
TERMINAL — Run after every reboot
# Set maximum power mode (mode 0 = full 15W for Orin Nano Super)
sudo nvpmodel -m 0

# Lock all clocks to maximum (CPU, GPU, memory)
sudo jetson_clocks

# Verify JetPack version (should show R36.x for JetPack 6.1)
cat /etc/nv_tegra_release

# Verify CUDA is working (should show "cuda release 12.6")
nvcc --version

# Check how much RAM is free (Jetson uses unified CPU+GPU memory)
free -h

# Check your Jetson's IP address (you'll need this for RTSP)
ip addr show eth0 | grep "inet "
✅
What nvpmodel -m 0 does: The Jetson has different "power modes" — low power (saves battery), balanced, and maximum. Mode 0 is maximum.

What jetson_clocks does: Even at max power mode, the Jetson might still lower CPU/GPU speed when idle to save power. jetson_clocks locks everything at full speed permanently until you reboot.

Connect via SSH (Optional but Recommended)

Once set up, you can control your Jetson from your laptop over the network. Much more convenient than using a physical keyboard.

From your laptop/PC
# Replace 192.168.1.10 with your Jetson's actual IP
# (you found this with "ip addr" in the step above)
ssh yourUsername@192.168.1.10

# Once connected, you're controlling the Jetson remotely
# All commands below can be run via SSH

Increase Swap Space (Important for First-Time Engine Build)

TensorRT engine compilation uses a lot of RAM. Adding swap space prevents crashes during the first build:

TERMINAL — Run once after setup
# Install zram-config for compressed swap
sudo apt-get install -y zram-config

# Or create a swap file (alternative method, 8GB swap)
sudo fallocate -l 8G /swapfile
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile

# Make it permanent (persists after reboot)
echo '/swapfile none swap sw 0 0' | sudo tee -a /etc/fstab

# Verify swap is active
free -h
# Should now show 8G in the Swap row

Full Software Installation

DeepStream, Ultralytics, and all dependencies — one after another

Step 4A — Update System Packages

# Always update first — gets you the latest security patches
sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get upgrade -y

# Install build tools and Python dependencies
sudo apt-get install -y \
    python3-pip \
    git \
    wget \
    curl \
    build-essential \
    libopencv-dev \
    python3-opencv \
    cmake

# Upgrade pip itself
pip3 install --upgrade pip setuptools wheel

Step 4B — Install DeepStream SDK 7.1

ℹ️
Where to get it: Go to catalog.ngc.nvidia.com → search "deepstream" → select "DeepStream SDK" → choose version 7.1 → download the Jetson .deb package. The file name will be like deepstream-7.1_7.1.0-1_arm64.deb
# Navigate to where you downloaded the .deb file
cd ~/Downloads

# Install prerequisites for DeepStream
sudo apt-get install -y \
    libssl-dev \
    libgstreamer1.0-dev \
    gstreamer1.0-tools \
    gstreamer1.0-plugins-good \
    gstreamer1.0-plugins-bad \
    gstreamer1.0-plugins-ugly \
    gstreamer1.0-libav \
    libgstrtspserver-1.0-dev \
    libjansson4 \
    libyaml-cpp-dev

# Install DeepStream from the downloaded .deb file
sudo apt-get install -y ./deepstream-7.1_7.1.0-1_arm64.deb

# Verify installation — you should see "DeepStream Version: 7.1.0"
deepstream-app --version-all

# Apply the RTSP manager fix (prevents stream freezing — do this now)
sudo /opt/nvidia/deepstream/deepstream/update_rtpmanager.sh

Step 4C — Install Ultralytics (YOLO)

# Clone the official Ultralytics repository
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/ultralytics/ultralytics
cd ultralytics

# Install with export extras [export] includes onnx, onnxruntime, etc.
pip install -e ".[export]"

# Install onnxslim separately (needed for DeepStream compatibility)
pip install onnxslim

# Verify — should print version like "8.x.x"
python3 -c "import ultralytics; print('Ultralytics version:', ultralytics.__version__)"

Step 4D — Clone DeepStream-Yolo Repository

# Clone the DeepStream-Yolo repo (this has the export26 script + config files)
cd ~
git clone https://github.com/marcoslucianops/DeepStream-Yolo

# See what's inside
ls ~/DeepStream-Yolo/

# You should see these important files and folders:
# config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt  ← AI model config
# deepstream_app_config.txt        ← main pipeline config
# labels.txt                       ← COCO class names (person, car, etc.)
# nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo/      ← C++ plugin source code
# utils/export_yolo26.py           ← the export script we need

YOLO26 Model Export — Converting YOLO to DeepStream Format

Download the model, run the export script, copy files to the right place

Step 5A — Copy the Export Script

# Copy the special yolo26 export script from DeepStream-Yolo into ultralytics folder
cp ~/DeepStream-Yolo/utils/export_yolo26.py ~/ultralytics/

# Go into the ultralytics folder (run the script from here)
cd ~/ultralytics

Step 5B — Choose and Download Your YOLO Model

ModelSizeSpeed (FP16)AccuracyBest For
yolo11n.pt2.6MB~190 FPSLower8+ streams, fastest response needed
yolo11s.pt ✓9.4MB~126 FPSGoodRecommended for most CCTV setups
yolo11m.pt20MB~64 FPSBetterImportant areas, need better detection
yolo11l.pt25MB~50 FPSHighCritical security, can afford lower FPS
# Download YOLO11s (recommended) — the "s" means "small" = best for Jetson Orin Nano
wget https://github.com/ultralytics/assets/releases/download/v8.3.0/yolo11s.pt

# Verify the download
ls -lh yolo11s.pt
# Should show: -rw-rw-r-- 1 ... 9.4M ... yolo11s.pt

Step 5C — Export to ONNX Using the YOLO26 Script

🎓
What the export options mean:
-w yolo11s.pt → which model file to convert
--simplify → clean up the model graph (always use this!)
--dynamic → allow variable batch size (for multiple streams)
-s 1280 720 → input video resolution (optional, default 640×640)
Standard export (recommended for most cases)
python3 export_yolo26.py -w yolo11s.pt --simplify --dynamic
Export for 1080p CCTV cameras (higher resolution)
python3 export_yolo26.py -w yolo11s.pt --simplify --dynamic -s 1920 1080
Export for 720p CCTV cameras (faster processing)
python3 export_yolo26.py -w yolo11s.pt --simplify --dynamic -s 1280 720
Verify export succeeded
ls -lh *.onnx
# Should see: yolo11s.pt.onnx  (around 17-20MB)

Step 5D — Copy Files to DeepStream-Yolo Folder

# Copy the ONNX model and labels file
cp ~/ultralytics/yolo11s.pt.onnx ~/DeepStream-Yolo/
cp ~/ultralytics/labels.txt ~/DeepStream-Yolo/

# Go to the working directory
cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo

# Confirm all needed files are here
ls -la
# You must see: yolo11s.pt.onnx, labels.txt, config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt,
#               deepstream_app_config.txt, nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo/ folder
8

Compiling the Custom YOLO Parser Library

Build the C++ plugin that lets DeepStream understand YOLO output format

ℹ️
Why is this needed? YOLO produces output in its own format (a tensor with box coordinates + confidence scores). DeepStream by default doesn't know how to read this format. This library is a "translator" that converts YOLO output into boxes DeepStream can draw on screen.
# Make sure you're in the DeepStream-Yolo folder
cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo

# ← IMPORTANT: Set the CUDA version for DeepStream 7.1 on JetPack 6.1
export CUDA_VER=12.6

# Compile: clean old build files first, then compile fresh
make -C nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo clean && make -C nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo

# Verify the compiled library was created successfully
ls -lh nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo/libnvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo.so
# Should show the .so file at around 1-2MB
⚠️
If you get errors:
• "nvcc not found" → Run: export PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.6/bin:$PATH
• "build-essential" error → Run: sudo apt-get install build-essential
• "Cannot find -lcuda" → Run: export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.6/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
9

Config Deep Dive: config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt

Every single field explained in plain English with examples for different scenarios

🎓
What this file does: This config tells DeepStream about the AI model — where to find it, how to read it, what resolution to use, and how confident a detection must be before it's shown. Edit this file with: nano ~/DeepStream-Yolo/config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt

Complete config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt with Explanations

config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt — Full annotated version
[property]

###############################################################
##  GPU AND MODEL LOADING
###############################################################

gpu-id=0
# Which GPU to use. On Jetson there is only ONE GPU, so this is always 0.
# Only change if you have a multi-GPU desktop (not applicable to Jetson).

net-scale-factor=0.0039215697906911373
# This is exactly 1/255.0
# Camera pixels have values 0-255. YOLO expects values 0.0-1.0.
# This number multiplies each pixel value to normalize it.
# Example: pixel value 255 × 0.00392... = 1.0
# DO NOT CHANGE THIS for standard YOLO models.

model-color-format=0
# Color channel order of the input image.
# 0 = RGB (Red, Green, Blue) ← YOLO was trained with RGB, use this
# 1 = BGR (Blue, Green, Red) ← OpenCV default, but NOT what YOLO uses
# 2 = GRAYSCALE ← for black and white only
# WRONG FORMAT = wrong colors = bad detections. Keep at 0.

onnx-file=yolo11s.pt.onnx
# ← PATH TO YOUR ONNX MODEL. This is the file created by export_yolo26.py.
# Path is relative to where you run deepstream-app from.
# If running from ~/DeepStream-Yolo/ then just the filename is fine.
# Absolute path example: /home/yourname/DeepStream-Yolo/yolo11s.pt.onnx

model-engine-file=model_b1_gpu0_fp16.engine
# ← The TensorRT compiled engine file.
# On FIRST RUN: this file doesn't exist yet. TensorRT will CREATE it.
# On subsequent runs: TensorRT loads this cached file (starts in seconds).
# File name convention: model_b{batch}_gpu{gpu}_{precision}.engine
# For FP16: model_b1_gpu0_fp16.engine
# For FP32: model_b1_gpu0_fp32.engine
# For 4 streams (batch 4): model_b4_gpu0_fp16.engine

labelfile-path=labels.txt
# ← Path to the text file with class names.
# This file has 80 lines (for COCO dataset): person, bicycle, car, ...
# Line 1 = class 0, Line 2 = class 1, etc.
# If you have a custom model with different objects, replace this file.
# Default labels.txt is in ~/DeepStream-Yolo/ after export.

int8-calib-file=calib.table
# INT8 calibration file. NOT used with JetPack 6.1 / TensorRT 10.x.
# Leave this line in or comment it out — it's ignored unless network-mode=1.

###############################################################
##  INPUT DIMENSIONS
###############################################################

infer-dims=3;640;640
# ← Input size: channels;height;width
# 3 = RGB (3 color channels). Do not change.
# 640;640 = default YOLO input size. This MUST match what you used in export!
# If you exported with -s 1920 1080, set this to 3;1080;1920
# If you exported with -s 1280 720, set this to 3;720;1280
# MISMATCH = crash or wrong detections.

###############################################################
##  PERFORMANCE: BATCH AND PRECISION
###############################################################

batch-size=1
# How many frames the GPU processes at once.
# SET THIS TO THE NUMBER OF CAMERA STREAMS.
# 1 camera  → batch-size=1
# 4 cameras → batch-size=4  (much more GPU efficient!)
# 8 cameras → batch-size=8
# Must also match batch-size in deepstream_app_config.txt [streammux] section.

network-mode=2
# Precision for inference calculations.
# 0 = FP32 (full precision, slowest, most accurate)
# 1 = INT8 (8-bit integers, fastest, slight accuracy loss)
#         → NOT supported on JetPack 6.1 / TensorRT 10.x!
# 2 = FP16 (half precision, 2× faster than FP32, nearly same accuracy) ← USE THIS
# For Jetson Orin Nano Super: ALWAYS use 2 (FP16).

###############################################################
##  DETECTION THRESHOLDS
###############################################################

num-detected-classes=80
# ← How many object classes your model detects.
# Standard YOLO11 trained on COCO dataset = 80 classes.
# If using a custom model (e.g. only detects "person" and "vehicle"),
# change this to match the number of classes in your custom labels.txt.

cluster-mode=2
# Method for combining overlapping detection boxes (NMS = Non-Maximum Suppression).
# 0 = OpenCV groupRectangles (old method)
# 1 = DBSCAN clustering
# 2 = NMS ← Standard for YOLO, use this
# 3 = No clustering (keep all boxes)
# 4 = NMS with groupRectangles for small objects

###############################################################
##  CUSTOM PARSER (Do not change these)
###############################################################

parse-bbox-func-name=NvDsInferParseYolo
# The function name inside the custom library that parses YOLO boxes.
# This exact name must match a function in the .so library you compiled.

custom-lib-path=nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo/libnvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo.so
# Path to the compiled plugin library.
# This is the .so file you built in Step 6.
# Path is relative to where you run deepstream-app from.

###############################################################
##  POST-PROCESSING THRESHOLDS
###############################################################

[class-attrs-all]
# Settings that apply to ALL detected classes (all 80 object types).
# You can override per-class with [class-attrs-0], [class-attrs-1], etc.

nms-iou-threshold=0.45
# IOU = "Intersection Over Union" — how much two boxes overlap.
# If two boxes for the SAME object overlap by more than this %, keep only the best one.
# 0.45 = if boxes overlap >45%, they're likely the same object → remove duplicate.
# Lower (0.3) = more aggressive de-duplication (can remove real separate objects)
# Higher (0.6) = keep more boxes (can show duplicate boxes on same object)
# For CCTV with people standing close together: try 0.5-0.6

pre-cluster-threshold=0.25
# Minimum confidence score before a detection is even considered.
# The AI scores each detection 0.0-1.0 (0%=not confident, 100%=very confident).
# 0.25 = only show detections where AI is >25% confident.
# Too low (0.1): many false detections (chair detected as person, etc.)
# Too high (0.7): miss real objects in poor lighting or at distance
# For daytime CCTV: 0.4-0.5 recommended
# For night / IR cameras: 0.2-0.3 to catch low-confidence detections
# For entry-point security (must catch everything): 0.15-0.25

Threshold Settings for Different CCTV Scenarios

Scenariopre-cluster-thresholdnms-iou-thresholdWhy
Daytime outdoor parking0.450.45Good light, clear view
Night IR cameras0.200.50Lower confidence in IR
Entrance/exit counting0.300.40Can't miss anyone
Crowded area (many people)0.350.60People close together
Far-away cameras (small objects)0.150.45Small objects = lower score
High-accuracy critical zones0.550.45Only very confident detections

Config Deep Dive: deepstream_app_config.txt

The pipeline config — every section explained with beginner-friendly detail

🎓
What this file does: This is the "main control panel" for the DeepStream pipeline. It defines: where to get video input (cameras), how to process it (resolution, batch), what AI model to use, and where to send output (screen, RTSP, file). Edit with: nano ~/DeepStream-Yolo/deepstream_app_config.txt

Section: [application]

[application]
enable-perf-stats=1
# 1 = print FPS performance statistics every few seconds in the terminal.
# You'll see lines like: **PERF: FPS Avg (Sink 0): 45.2**
# 0 = silent mode (no FPS output)
# Keep at 1 while testing so you can see if performance is good.

perf-measurement-interval-sec=5
# How often (in seconds) to print the FPS stats. 5 = every 5 seconds.

Section: [tiled-display]

[tiled-display]
enable=1
# 1 = show streams as a grid (tiled view). 0 = show only one stream.

rows=1
# Number of rows in the grid.
# 1 camera  → rows=1, columns=1
# 4 cameras → rows=2, columns=2  (2×2 grid)
# 6 cameras → rows=2, columns=3  (2×3 grid)
# 8 cameras → rows=2, columns=4  or rows=4, columns=2

columns=1

width=1280
# Total WIDTH of the whole tiled display (not per-tile width).
# For 1080p monitor: 1920. For 4K monitor: 3840.
# Each tile gets width÷columns pixels. E.g. 1280 ÷ 2 cols = 640px per tile.

height=720
# Total HEIGHT of the whole tiled display.
# For 1080p monitor: 1080. Each tile gets height÷rows pixels.

Section: [source0] — Where Does Video Come From?

[source0]
enable=1
# 1 = this source is active. 0 = disabled/skip this source.

type=4
# ← MOST IMPORTANT FIELD: what kind of input is this?
# 1 = Camera device (like /dev/video0 — USB webcam directly connected)
# 2 = URI — a single file or RTSP URL directly as one stream
# 3 = URI (multi-source) — use when adding num-sources>1 in same block
# 4 = RTSP (live stream) — for IP cameras over network ← USE THIS FOR CCTV
# TYPE 4 is specifically optimized for live RTSP (auto-reconnects on drop)

num-sources=1
# How many streams does this source block handle?
# Usually keep at 1 per [source] block.
# If using type=3, you can set num-sources=4 and add 4 uri= lines.

uri=rtsp://admin:password@192.168.1.101:554/stream1
# ← THE RTSP URL OF YOUR CAMERA.
# Format: rtsp://USERNAME:PASSWORD@IP_ADDRESS:PORT/STREAM_PATH
# If no password: rtsp://192.168.1.101:554/stream1
# Default RTSP port is 554 but some cameras use 8554.
# FIND YOUR CAMERA'S URL in its web interface or manual.
# Common URLs by brand:
#   Hikvision: rtsp://admin:pass@IP:554/Streaming/Channels/101
#   Dahua:     rtsp://admin:pass@IP:554/cam/realmonitor?channel=1&subtype=0
#   Axis:      rtsp://root:pass@IP/axis-media/media.amp
#   Generic:   rtsp://admin:pass@IP:554/stream1  or /live

cudadec-memtype=0
# Where in memory to store decoded video frames.
# 0 = GPU device memory (fastest for Jetson — keep this)
# 1 = pinned (CPU-accessible) memory
# 2 = unified memory (accessible by both CPU and GPU)
# Jetson has unified CPU+GPU memory architecture, but 0 is still fastest.

drop-frame-interval=0
# Skip every N frames to reduce processing load.
# 0 = process EVERY frame (default)
# 1 = process every 2nd frame (halves GPU load)
# 2 = process every 3rd frame
# For 30fps camera with 4 streams on Orin Nano: start with 0.
# If FPS drops too low, increase this to 1 or 2.

latency=100
# RTSP receive buffer size in milliseconds.
# 100ms = small buffer, low delay, might drop frames on slow network.
# 500ms = larger buffer, higher delay, more stable for bad networks.
# For local network (same room): 100ms is fine.
# For camera on different floor/building: use 200-500ms.
# For camera over internet/VPN: use 1000-2000ms.

select-rtp-protocol=0
# Transport protocol for the RTSP stream.
# 0 = Auto (tries UDP first, falls back to TCP)
# 1 = UDP only (lower latency, but packets can drop)
# 2 = UDP multicast (for one-to-many streaming)
# 4 = TCP only (more reliable, slightly higher latency)
# If your stream keeps freezing/disconnecting: change to 4 (TCP).

Section: [streammux] — The Stream Combiner

[streammux]
batch-size=1
# ← MUST EQUAL the total number of active camera streams.
# 1 camera = 1, 4 cameras = 4, 8 cameras = 8.
# This and batch-size in config_infer must ALWAYS match.

width=1920
# The width ALL streams are resized to before going into the AI model.
# Must match or be divisible by the ONNX model's infer-dims.
# If your camera is 1080p: set 1920. If 720p: set 1280.
# This is the INTERNAL processing resolution, not the display resolution.

height=1080

live-source=1
# ← CRITICAL: Set to 1 for RTSP (live) streams, 0 for file inputs!
# When set to 1: streammux won't wait for slow sources, won't buffer too much.
# If you forget this for RTSP: you'll get high latency or freezes.

batched-push-timeout=40000
# Time in microseconds (not milliseconds!) to wait for all streams to provide
# a frame before processing the batch anyway.
# 40000 µs = 40ms = handles up to 25fps cameras.
# For 30fps cameras: 33333 µs.
# If one camera disconnects and others freeze: increase to 400000.

enable-padding=0
# 0 = stretch/squish the camera image to fit the processing resolution
# 1 = letterbox (keep aspect ratio, add black bars)
# 0 is faster. 1 preserves aspect ratio (better for accurate detection).

Section: [primary-gie] — Which AI Model to Use

[primary-gie]
enable=1
# 1 = run this AI model. Always 1.

config-file=config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt
# ← Path to the inference config file (Section 07 in this guide).
# This links the two config files together.

gpu-id=0
# Always 0 on Jetson.

batch-size=1
# Must match the batch-size in config_infer AND in [streammux].
# All three must be the same number.

Section: [sink0] — Where Does Output Go?

# ═══ OPTION A: Show on connected HDMI display ═══
[sink0]
enable=1
type=2
# 1 = FakeSink (no output — runs AI but throws away video, useful for testing)
# 2 = EglSink (display window on a connected HDMI/DP monitor) ← ON-SCREEN
# 3 = FileSink (encode and save to video file)
# 4 = RTSP output (stream the annotated video over RTSP to another machine)
sync=0
# 0 = run as fast as possible (ignores video timestamps). Best for max FPS.
# 1 = sync to video clock (smooth playback but limits to camera FPS).
display-id=0
# Which display to use (0 = default/first display).
offset-x=0
# X position of the display window in pixels from left edge.
offset-y=0
# Y position of the display window in pixels from top edge.
width=1280
# Width of the DISPLAY WINDOW (not the processing resolution).
height=720
# Height of the display window.
gpu-id=0

config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt key settings:

[property]
gpu-id=0
net-scale-factor=0.0039215697906911373
model-color-format=0
onnx-file=yolo11s.pt.onnx
model-engine-file=model_b1_gpu0_fp16.engine
labelfile-path=labels.txt
infer-dims=3;640;640
batch-size=1
network-mode=2
# FP16
num-detected-classes=80
cluster-mode=2
parse-bbox-func-name=NvDsInferParseYolo

[class-attrs-all]
nms-iou-threshold=0.45
pre-cluster-threshold=0.25

Run it:

cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt

# First run: TensorRT builds the engine (5-15 minutes, shows no output)
# After building: you'll see "**PERF: FPS Avg (Sink 0): XX.X**" every 5 sec
# Your HDMI monitor should show the camera feed with detection boxes!
✅
No CCTV camera yet? Test with a local video file: In [source0] set type=3 and uri=file:///path/to/video.mp4. Also change live-source=0 in [streammux]. Sample videos are in /opt/nvidia/deepstream/deepstream/samples/streams/

Edge Jetson 1 (IP: 192.168.1.10) ingests 4 cameras, runs YOLO, and outputs ONE annotated RTSP stream showing a 2×2 tiled view of all 4 cameras with detection boxes drawn.

Part C-2: Configure Edge Jetson 2 (Zone B — Cameras 5-8)

Edge Jetson 2 is identical to Jetson 1 but with cameras 5-8 IP addresses and its own IP (192.168.1.11). The deepstream_app_config.txt is the same structure — just replace the IP addresses in [source0] through [source3]:

# On Edge Jetson 2, change the source URIs:
[source0] uri=rtsp://admin:pass@192.168.1.105:554/stream  # Camera 5
[source1] uri=rtsp://admin:pass@192.168.1.106:554/stream  # Camera 6
[source2] uri=rtsp://admin:pass@192.168.1.107:554/stream  # Camera 7
[source3] uri=rtsp://admin:pass@192.168.1.108:554/stream  # Camera 8

# Everything else stays the same!
# The RTSP output will be at: rtsp://192.168.1.11:8554/ds-test

Part C-3: Configure the Master Jetson (Aggregator)

The master Jetson (192.168.1.5) receives the 2 RTSP streams from the edge Jetsons and displays them side by side on a monitor. Since the edge Jetsons already ran YOLO, the master just needs to display — no AI needed. But we keep DeepStream running for the tiled display capability.

# ─── Source: RTSP from Edge Jetson 2 ────────────────────────

# ← The RTSP output stream of Edge Jetson 2
cudadec-memtype=0
latency=200

[streammux]
batch-size=2
# 2 sources = batch size 2
width=1920
height=1080
batched-push-timeout=100000
# Higher timeout — network latency between Jetsons
live-source=1

[primary-gie]
enable=1
config-file=config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt
gpu-id=0
batch-size=2

[sink0]
enable=1
type=2
# 2 = Display on HDMI monitor connected to master Jetson
sync=0
display-id=0
offset-x=0
offset-y=0
width=1920
height=1080
gpu-id=0
⚠️
Start edge Jetsons FIRST. Wait 15-30 seconds for their RTSP streams to be available, THEN start the master Jetson. The master needs the streams to already be running when it starts.

Startup Order (Very Important)

1

Start all 4 Edge Jetsons first

SSH into each edge Jetson and run: cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo && deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt &. The & runs it in the background.

2

Wait for edge Jetsons to finish building engines (first time only)

Watch for "PERF: FPS Avg" lines in their terminal output. This means the engine is built and RTSP is streaming.

3

Verify RTSP streams are accessible from master Jetson

gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test" ! decodebin ! fakesink. Should print data rate without errors.

4

Start the Master Jetson

cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo && deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt on the master. The 4K display should show all zones.

15

Making Jetson Output an RTSP Stream

Full config to stream annotated video over the network — accessible from any device

🎓
What RTSP output means: Instead of showing detection results on a monitor connected to the Jetson, the Jetson hosts an RTSP server. Any device on the same network can then "tune in" to that stream — a laptop, VLC player, NVR software, another Jetson, or even a phone app.

Full RTSP Output Configuration

sink section in deepstream_app_config.txt — RTSP OUTPUT
[sink0]
enable=1
type=4
# 4 = RTSP output sink. DeepStream becomes an RTSP server.
sync=0

codec=1
# Video encoding format for the output stream.
# 1 = H.264 (most compatible — works with VLC, most CCTV software, phones)
# 2 = H.265 (HEVC — better quality at same bitrate, but some devices can't decode)
# Use 1 (H.264) unless you specifically need H.265.

bitrate=4000000
# Output video bitrate in bits-per-second.
# 4000000 = 4 Mbps → good quality for 1080p
# For 720p output: 2000000 (2 Mbps)
# For 4 streams tiled into one: 6-8 Mbps recommended
# Higher bitrate = better quality but more network bandwidth needed
# Your network switch must handle: bitrate × number of simultaneous viewers

enc-type=0
# 0 = hardware encoder (uses Jetson's built-in video encoder — fast, low CPU)
# 1 = software encoder (uses CPU — slower, avoid on Jetson)
# Always 0 on Jetson.

rtsp-port=8554
# TCP port for the RTSP server.
# 8554 is the standard RTSP port (different from camera's 554 to avoid conflict).
# You can change this if port 8554 is blocked by firewall.
# The full URL becomes: rtsp://<JETSON_IP>:8554/ds-test

udp-port=5400
# UDP port used for the actual video data transfer.
# Usually set to rtsp-port - 3154 (8554 - 3154 = 5400).
# Must not conflict with other services. If you run multiple DeepStream
# instances on one Jetson: use different udp-ports (5400, 5401, 5402...).

# ─── To also display ON-SCREEN while streaming RTSP ──────────
[sink1]
# You can have BOTH outputs at once!
enable=1
type=2
# Local HDMI display
sync=0
display-id=0
offset-x=0
offset-y=0
width=1280
height=720
gpu-id=0

How to Access the RTSP Stream from Another Device

VLC Media Player (any computer/laptop)
# Open VLC → Media → Open Network Stream → paste this URL:
rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test
# Replace 192.168.1.10 with your Jetson's actual IP address
GStreamer (test from command line)
gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test" latency=200 ! decodebin ! autovideosink
ffplay (part of FFmpeg)
ffplay rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test
Open on Android/iPhone — VLC Mobile App
# Install VLC from App Store / Google Play
# Open VLC → Network → New Stream → Enter:
rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test
# (your phone must be on the same WiFi network as the Jetson)

Finding Your Jetson's IP Address

# On the Jetson terminal:
ip addr show eth0 | grep "inet "
# Shows something like: inet 192.168.1.10/24
# The number before /24 is your IP (e.g. 192.168.1.10)

# OR simpler:
hostname -I
# Prints all IPs. First one is usually the main network IP.
✅
Open firewall port (if RTSP not accessible):
sudo ufw allow 8554/tcp && sudo ufw allow 5400/udp
Then verify firewall rules: sudo ufw status
16

Viewing All RTSP Streams on One Display

Multiple methods — from simple VLC to a full monitoring dashboard

Method 1 — VLC Mosaic View (Simplest)

VLC on your laptop/PC can display multiple RTSP streams in a grid. Open multiple VLC instances and arrange windows, OR use VLC's mosaic filter (advanced).

Quick multi-stream view with VLC (open 4 windows)
# Open 4 separate VLC windows — simple approach:
vlc rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test &
vlc rtsp://192.168.1.11:8554/ds-test &
vlc rtsp://192.168.1.12:8554/ds-test &
vlc rtsp://192.168.1.13:8554/ds-test &
# Manually arrange the windows on your screen

Method 2 — Python + OpenCV Multi-Stream Viewer

A simple Python script that reads all RTSP streams and shows them in a grid on one window. Run this on the master Jetson or any computer:

Save as ~/view_streams.py
import cv2
import threading
import numpy as np
import time

# ─── CONFIGURE THESE ────────────────────────────────────────
STREAMS = [
    "rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test",   # Edge Jetson 1 (Zone A)
    "rtsp://192.168.1.11:8554/ds-test",   # Edge Jetson 2 (Zone B)
    "rtsp://192.168.1.12:8554/ds-test",   # Edge Jetson 3 (Zone C)
    "rtsp://192.168.1.13:8554/ds-test",   # Edge Jetson 4 (Zone D)
]
GRID_COLS = 2              # Columns in the display grid
TILE_W, TILE_H = 960, 540  # Size of each tile in pixels
# ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

frames = [None] * len(STREAMS)
running = True

def capture_stream(idx, url):
    cap = cv2.VideoCapture(url)
    cap.set(cv2.CAP_PROP_BUFFERSIZE, 1)  # Low latency buffer
    while running:
        ret, frame = cap.read()
        if ret:
            frames[idx] = cv2.resize(frame, (TILE_W, TILE_H))
        else:
            # Connection lost — show error tile
            err = np.zeros((TILE_H, TILE_W, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
            cv2.putText(err, f"DISCONNECTED: {url.split('@')[-1]}",
                       (20, TILE_H//2), cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX,
                       0.6, (0, 0, 255), 2)
            frames[idx] = err
            time.sleep(2)
            cap.release()
            cap = cv2.VideoCapture(url)  # Try to reconnect
    cap.release()

# Start one thread per stream
threads = []
for i, url in enumerate(STREAMS):
    t = threading.Thread(target=capture_stream, args=(i, url), daemon=True)
    t.start()
    threads.append(t)

print("Starting multi-stream viewer... Press 'q' to quit.")
time.sleep(2)  # Wait for streams to connect

while True:
    # Build the grid
    grid_rows = []
    n = len(STREAMS)
    cols = GRID_COLS
    rows = (n + cols - 1) // cols  # Ceiling division

    for r in range(rows):
        row_tiles = []
        for c in range(cols):
            idx = r * cols + c
            if idx < n and frames[idx] is not None:
                tile = frames[idx].copy()
            else:
                tile = np.zeros((TILE_H, TILE_W, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
            # Add stream label
            label = f"Jetson {idx+1}" if idx < n else ""
            cv2.putText(tile, label, (10, 30),
                       cv2.FONT_HERSHEY_SIMPLEX, 1.0, (0, 255, 0), 2)
            row_tiles.append(tile)
        grid_rows.append(np.hstack(row_tiles))

    grid = np.vstack(grid_rows)
    cv2.imshow("YOLO CCTV Monitor", grid)

    if cv2.waitKey(1) & 0xFF == ord('q'):
        running = False
        break

cv2.destroyAllWindows()
print("Viewer closed.")
Run the viewer
# Install OpenCV if not already installed
pip3 install opencv-python

# Run the viewer (needs a display connected)
python3 ~/view_streams.py

# Press 'q' to quit

Method 3 — MediaMTX (Powerful RTSP Relay + HLS Web View)

MediaMTX is a free server that can receive RTSP streams and re-broadcast them. You can even view streams in a web browser with no VLC needed:

# Install MediaMTX on the master Jetson
cd ~
wget https://github.com/bluenviron/mediamtx/releases/latest/download/mediamtx_linux_arm64.tar.gz
tar -xzf mediamtx_linux_arm64.tar.gz
chmod +x mediamtx

# Create a simple config (mediamtx.yml)
cat > mediamtx.yml << 'EOF'
paths:
  zone-a:
    source: rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test
  zone-b:
    source: rtsp://192.168.1.11:8554/ds-test
  zone-c:
    source: rtsp://192.168.1.12:8554/ds-test
  zone-d:
    source: rtsp://192.168.1.13:8554/ds-test
EOF

# Run MediaMTX
./mediamtx mediamtx.yml

# Now access in browser (from any computer on network):
# http://192.168.1.5:8888/zone-a    ← Zone A HLS stream
# http://192.168.1.5:8888/zone-b    ← Zone B HLS stream
# Or as RTSP from other tools: rtsp://192.168.1.5:8554/zone-a

Method 4 — DeepStream on Master Jetson (Already Covered in Scenarios C & D)

The most powerful option — use DeepStream on the master Jetson to receive all RTSP streams and display them in a tiled grid on a connected monitor. This is what Scenarios C and D show. DeepStream's tiled display is zero-copy on Jetson's unified memory, making it very efficient.

17

Network Setup & IP Addressing

How to connect everything properly — switches, static IPs, bandwidth planning

Physical Network Setup

🔌 What you need

  • Gigabit network switch (1Gbps)
  • Cat6 ethernet cables (one per device)
  • PoE switch (optional — powers cameras over ethernet)
  • Router (connects to internet for updates)

📡 Bandwidth per camera (approx)

  • 1080p H.264 camera: 4-8 Mbps
  • 720p H.264 camera: 2-4 Mbps
  • Jetson RTSP output: 4-8 Mbps
  • 1Gbps switch handles 100+ cameras
  • Use dedicated CCTV VLAN if possible

Setting Static IP Addresses on Jetson

Static IPs ensure your Jetson always has the same address. Without this, the IP might change after a reboot and your RTSP URLs would break.

# Method 1: Using nmcli (recommended on JetPack 6.x)

# First, find your connection name
nmcli connection show
# Look for something like "Wired connection 1" or "eth0"

# Set static IP for Edge Jetson 1 (example: 192.168.1.10)
sudo nmcli connection modify "Wired connection 1" \
    ipv4.method manual \
    ipv4.addresses 192.168.1.10/24 \
    ipv4.gateway 192.168.1.1 \
    ipv4.dns "8.8.8.8,8.8.4.4"

# Apply the changes
sudo nmcli connection up "Wired connection 1"

# Verify the new IP
ip addr show eth0
# Should now show "inet 192.168.1.10/24"

# ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Repeat for each Jetson with different IP:
# Edge Jetson 1: 192.168.1.10
# Edge Jetson 2: 192.168.1.11
# Edge Jetson 3: 192.168.1.12
# Edge Jetson 4: 192.168.1.13
# Master Jetson:  192.168.1.5

Auto-Start DeepStream on Boot

For a production deployment, you want DeepStream to start automatically when the Jetson powers on:

# Create a startup script
cat > ~/start_deepstream.sh << 'EOF'
#!/bin/bash
# Wait for network to be ready
sleep 15

# Set maximum performance
sudo nvpmodel -m 0
sudo jetson_clocks

# Start DeepStream
cd /home/yourUsername/DeepStream-Yolo
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt >> /var/log/deepstream.log 2>&1
EOF

chmod +x ~/start_deepstream.sh

# Create a systemd service to run at boot
sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/deepstream.service << 'EOF'
[Unit]
Description=DeepStream YOLO CCTV Service
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
User=yourUsername
ExecStart=/home/yourUsername/start_deepstream.sh
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=10

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
EOF

# Enable and start the service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl enable deepstream.service
sudo systemctl start deepstream.service

# Check status
sudo systemctl status deepstream.service
18

Troubleshooting — Every Common Problem Solved

Detailed explanations and step-by-step fixes

Problem 1: First run takes forever / seems stuck

⚠️
This is completely normal. TensorRT is building the optimized engine file. For yolo11s on Orin Nano Super: expect 8–20 minutes. No output in the terminal is expected during this time. Only ONE core runs at 100% (this is normal). Do NOT press Ctrl+C — let it finish.
# To see that it IS working (in a second terminal):
watch -n 2 ls -lh ~/DeepStream-Yolo/*.engine
# A .engine file will appear and grow in size while building

# After building, you'll see FPS output:
# **PERF:  Source 0 FPS: 45.2 (Avg FPS: 45.0, #Frames: 225)

Problem 2: RTSP stream freezes or shows "EOS Error"

# Fix 1: Apply the RTSP manager patch (must do this once)
sudo /opt/nvidia/deepstream/deepstream/update_rtpmanager.sh

# Fix 2: Switch to TCP protocol in the source config
# In deepstream_app_config.txt, change:
select-rtp-protocol=4   # 4 = TCP only (most reliable)

# Fix 3: Increase the jitter buffer
latency=500   # Was 100, increase to 500ms

# Fix 4: Verify the camera stream works independently
gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://admin:pass@IP:554/stream" ! decodebin ! fakesink
# If this also fails, the problem is the camera, not DeepStream

Problem 3: "Cannot parse model" or ONNX errors

# Re-export the model with --simplify (REQUIRED for DeepStream 7.1)
cd ~/ultralytics
python3 export_yolo26.py -w yolo11s.pt --simplify --dynamic

# Delete old engine and ONNX files first
rm -f ~/DeepStream-Yolo/*.onnx ~/DeepStream-Yolo/*.engine

# Copy fresh ONNX
cp ~/ultralytics/yolo11s.pt.onnx ~/DeepStream-Yolo/

Problem 4: CUDA version error during make

# Error: "CUDA_VER not set" or "nvcc not found"
# Fix: Set the correct paths before compiling
export CUDA_VER=12.6
export PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.6/bin:$PATH
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/usr/local/cuda-12.6/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH

# Then recompile
cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo
make -C nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo clean && make -C nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo

Problem 5: Low FPS (under 15 per stream)

CauseCheckFix
Power mode not setRun nvpmodel -qsudo nvpmodel -m 0 && sudo jetson_clocks
FP32 instead of FP16Check network-mode in config_inferSet network-mode=2
Too many streams for model sizeCount sources vs batch-sizeUse yolo11n instead of yolo11s
Camera resolution too highCheck infer-dimsExport model at 640×640, not 1920×1080
Processing every frameCheck drop-frame-intervalSet drop-frame-interval=1 or 2

Problem 6: Cannot access RTSP output from another device

# Check if the RTSP port is open on the Jetson
sudo ss -tlnp | grep 8554
# Should show deepstream-app listening on port 8554

# Open the firewall port
sudo ufw allow 8554/tcp
sudo ufw allow 5400/udp

# Test from another device (ping first)
ping 192.168.1.10
# Then try: ffplay rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test

# If ping fails: check ethernet cable and switch port LEDs

Problem 7: GLib pthread error on startup

# Error: "GLib-ERROR: createdat: /usr/include/c++/11/bits/..."
# Fix: Upgrade glib2.0 to 2.76.6+
sudo apt-get install -y libglib2.0-dev
# Or follow DeepStream-Yolo Notes for manual glib upgrade

Problem 8: Wrong detections / detecting wrong objects

# Verify labels.txt is correct and in the right path
cat ~/DeepStream-Yolo/labels.txt | head -5
# Should show: person, bicycle, car, motorcycle, airplane...

# Verify labelfile-path in config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt
grep labelfile ~/DeepStream-Yolo/config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt
# Should show: labelfile-path=labels.txt

# Verify model-color-format is 0 (RGB)
grep model-color ~/DeepStream-Yolo/config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt
# Must be: model-color-format=0

Problem 9: One of the edge Jetsons drops out

# Check if DeepStream is still running on the edge Jetson
ssh user@192.168.1.10 "ps aux | grep deepstream"

# Check the log (if you set up autostart with our service)
ssh user@192.168.1.10 "tail -50 /var/log/deepstream.log"

# Restart the service on the edge Jetson
ssh user@192.168.1.10 "sudo systemctl restart deepstream"

# On the master Jetson: DeepStream will automatically try to reconnect
# to the RTSP source. The tile will be black while reconnecting.
# Reconnection happens automatically within ~30 seconds.

🎯 Complete YOLO26 Multi-Jetson CCTV Reference

JetPack 6.1 · DeepStream 7.1 · CUDA 12.6 · TensorRT 10.x · export_yolo26.py

Part 3

Jetson 3 — Selective Inference Architecture
Running inference on only 4 of 16 streams (Process A / B / C design).
YES — 100% POSSIBLE

Jetson 3: YOLO on 2 Streams +
Relay 2 Streams — No Double Detection

Complete reasoning, architecture, and every config file for running selective inference on one Jetson — local cameras get YOLO, relayed streams pass through clean.

3 Jetsons · 10 streams
Jetson 3: 2 YOLO + 2 relay
3 DeepStream instances
Combined display + RTSP
Website integration

✅ Yes — It Is 100% Possible. Here's Exactly Why.

DeepStream's nvinfer (the inference plugin) applies to all streams in its pipeline equally. You cannot tell a single DeepStream pipeline "run YOLO on source 0 and 1, but skip source 2 and 3." That is a real limitation.

But here's the solution: Run two separate DeepStream processes on Jetson 3 simultaneously. Process A handles your 2 local cameras with full YOLO inference. Process B handles the 2 relay RTSP streams from Jetsons 1 and 2 — with inference completely disabled — it just receives, tiles, and re-streams. Then a third lightweight Process C combines all four outputs into one tiled display and one RTSP stream for your website.

Jetson Orin Nano Super has 8GB unified memory and a capable GPU. Running 3 DeepStream instances where only one instance does heavy YOLO inference is well within its capability.

❌ Why a Single DeepStream Pipeline Cannot Do This

In a single DeepStream pipeline: all streams → streammux → one nvinfer plugin → all streams get inference applied uniformly. The nvinfer plugin has no source-id-filter or "skip inference for this source" config option.

You could set enable=0 in [primary-gie] — but that disables YOLO for ALL streams, not selectively. That means your 2 local cameras also lose detection. Not what you want.

Note: There is a secondary-gie that can operate on specific class IDs — but it can't filter by source ID either. The only true solution is separate pipelines.

ℹ️
Why does Process C have no YOLO? Streams coming into Process C are already annotated — Process A drew boxes on cams 9-10, Jetsons 1 and 2 drew boxes on cams 1-8. Running YOLO a third time would add duplicate boxes. So Process C is a pure combiner — it just tiles all 4 streams and outputs them.
20

Port Map — Jetson 3 Runs Three Separate Processes

Each process needs its own RTSP port and UDP port

ProcessRoleRTSP PortUDP PortURL
Jetson 3 — Process A YOLO on 2 local cameras 85565402 rtsp://192.168.1.12:8556/ds-test
Jetson 3 — Process B Relay J1+J2 streams (no inference) 85575403 rtsp://192.168.1.12:8557/ds-test
Jetson 3 — Process C Combine A+B → display + website RTSP 85585404 rtsp://192.168.1.12:8558/ds-test
Jetson 1YOLO on cameras 1-485545400rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test
Jetson 2YOLO on cameras 5-885545400rtsp://192.168.1.11:8554/ds-test
⚠️
Each process on Jetson 3 MUST use a different rtsp-port and udp-port. Two DeepStream processes cannot share the same port on the same machine — it will cause "Address already in use" errors. Use 8556, 8557, 8558 for the three processes on Jetson 3.

Separate Config Folders for Each Process

Directory structure on Jetson 3
~/DeepStream-Yolo/
├── process-a/                    # YOLO on local cameras 9 & 10
│   ├── deepstream_app_config.txt
│   └── config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt
│
├── process-b/                    # Relay streams from J1 & J2 — no inference
│   └── deepstream_app_config.txt  # (no config_infer needed)
│
├── process-c/                    # Combine A+B → HDMI + website RTSP
│   └── deepstream_app_config.txt  # (no config_infer needed)
│
├── yolo11s.pt.onnx               # Shared ONNX model (used by Process A only)
├── labels.txt
└── nvdsinfer_custom_impl_Yolo/   # Compiled .so (used by Process A only)

# Create the folders:
mkdir -p ~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-a
mkdir -p ~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-b
mkdir -p ~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-c

Process A — YOLO Inference on Local Cameras 9 & 10

Standard DeepStream with full YOLO, batch=2, outputs RTSP on port 8556

PROCESS A
Local cameras 9 & 10 → YOLO inference → RTSP :8556 batch=2 · FP16 · engine: model_b2_gpu0_fp16.engine
~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-a/deepstream_app_config.txt
[application]
enable-perf-stats=1
perf-measurement-interval-sec=5

[tiled-display]
enable=1
rows=1
columns=2
# 1×2 grid — 2 local cameras side by side
width=1920
height=540
# Half height — two cameras in a wide strip

# ── LOCAL CAMERA 9 ──────────────────────────────────────────
[source0]
enable=1
type=4
uri=rtsp://admin:pass@192.168.1.109:554/stream
# ← Camera 9 connected directly to this Jetson's network
num-sources=1
cudadec-memtype=0
latency=100
drop-frame-interval=0
select-rtp-protocol=4

# ── LOCAL CAMERA 10 ─────────────────────────────────────────
[source1]
enable=1
type=4
uri=rtsp://admin:pass@192.168.1.110:554/stream
# ← Camera 10
num-sources=1
cudadec-memtype=0
latency=100
drop-frame-interval=0
select-rtp-protocol=4

[streammux]
batch-size=2
# 2 local cameras = batch 2
width=1920
height=1080
batched-push-timeout=40000
live-source=1

# ── YOLO INFERENCE ENABLED ──────────────────────────────────
[primary-gie]
enable=1
# ← INFERENCE IS ON for this process
config-file=../process-a/config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt

batch-size=2

# ── RTSP OUTPUT ONLY (no local display — let Process C handle display) ──

# RTSP output — Process C will consume this
sync=0
codec=1
bitrate=4000000
enc-type=0

# ← Process A uses port 8556

# ← Unique UDP port for Process A
~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-a/config_infer_primary_yolo26.txt
[property]
gpu-id=0
net-scale-factor=0.0039215697906911373
model-color-format=0
onnx-file=../yolo11s.pt.onnx

[class-attrs-all]

pre-cluster-threshold=0.25

Process B — Relay Streams from Jetsons 1 & 2, Zero Inference

Receives already-annotated RTSP, tiles them, re-outputs as RTSP — no YOLO at all

PROCESS B
J1 :8554 + J2 :8554 → passthrough → RTSP :8557 NO inference · batch=2 · very lightweight
✅
This is the key to your requirement. By setting enable=0 in [primary-gie] for this process, DeepStream completely skips the inference step. The streams from Jetsons 1 and 2 — which already have detection boxes drawn on them — flow through unchanged. No double detection. No extra boxes. Clean passthrough.
~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-b/deepstream_app_config.txt
[application]
enable-perf-stats=1
perf-measurement-interval-sec=10

[tiled-display]
enable=1
rows=1
columns=2
# 1×2 grid for the 2 relay streams
width=1920
height=540

# ── RELAY STREAM FROM JETSON 1 ──────────────────────────────
[source0]
enable=1
type=4
uri=rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test
# ← Annotated output from Jetson 1 (cameras 1-4, 2×2 tiled)
num-sources=1
cudadec-memtype=0
latency=300
drop-frame-interval=0
select-rtp-protocol=4

# ── RELAY STREAM FROM JETSON 2 ──────────────────────────────
[source1]
enable=1
type=4
uri=rtsp://192.168.1.11:8554/ds-test
# ← Annotated output from Jetson 2 (cameras 5-8, 2×2 tiled)
num-sources=1
cudadec-memtype=0
latency=300
drop-frame-interval=0
select-rtp-protocol=4

[streammux]
batch-size=2
width=1920
height=1080
batched-push-timeout=200000
live-source=1

# ── INFERENCE COMPLETELY DISABLED FOR THIS PROCESS ──────────
[primary-gie]
enable=0
# ← THIS IS THE KEY LINE.
# enable=0 completely skips YOLO inference for ALL streams in this process.
# Streams from J1 and J2 pass through without any new detection boxes.
# Their existing boxes (drawn by J1/J2) are preserved in the video pixels.
# No config-file needed when enable=0.

# ── RTSP OUTPUT ─────────────────────────────────────────────
[sink0]
enable=1
type=4
sync=0
codec=1
bitrate=6000000
# 6 Mbps — J1/J2 outputs are already 2×2 tiled 1080p, need more bandwidth
enc-type=0
rtsp-port=8557
# ← Process B uses port 8557
udp-port=5403
# ← Unique UDP port for Process B
ℹ️
No config_infer file needed for Process B — since enable=0 in [primary-gie], DeepStream doesn't load any inference engine at all. This also means no engine-build wait time. Process B starts in seconds.
23

Process C — Combine All 4 → HDMI Display + Website RTSP

Takes Process A and Process B outputs, tiles into final view, dual sink output

PROCESS C
:8556 (cam 9-10) + :8557 (cam 1-8) → 2×2 display + RTSP :8558 NO inference · dual sink: type=2 + type=4
⚠️
Important tiling note: Process C receives:
• source0 (:8556) = a 1×2 strip showing cam 9 and cam 10 side by side
• source1 (:8557) = a 1×2 strip showing J1's 2×2 grid (cams 1-4) and J2's 2×2 grid (cams 5-8) side by side
In Process C's 2×2 grid: tile 0 = cams 9-10 strip, tile 1 = cams 1-8 strip. This gives a complete view of all 10 camera outputs in one display.
~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-c/deepstream_app_config.txt

How to Start All 3 Processes on Jetson 3

Correct order, separate terminals (or tmux), and the auto-start script

Option 1 — Manual Start (Testing)

Use 3 separate SSH sessions or tmux windows:

Terminal / SSH Session 1 — Start Process A first
# Terminal 1: Process A — YOLO on local cameras
cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-a
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt

# Watch for: "**PERF: FPS Avg (Sink 0): XX**"
# First run: 5-10 min (building model_b2_gpu0_fp16.engine)
Terminal / SSH Session 2 — Start Process B after A is streaming
# Terminal 2: Process B — relay J1+J2 streams (starts instantly, no engine build)
cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-b
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt

# Starts immediately. No engine build needed (GIE disabled).
# Watch for FPS output to confirm streams are flowing.
Terminal / SSH Session 3 — Start Process C last
# Terminal 3: Process C — combines A+B into display + RTSP for website
# Wait for Process A and B to both show FPS output before starting this.
export DISPLAY=:0     # Required for HDMI display sink
cd ~/DeepStream-Yolo/process-c
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt

# HDMI monitor should now show all streams.
# Website stream: rtsp://192.168.1.12:8558/ds-test

Option 2 — One-Shot Auto-Start Script (Production)

~/start_jetson3.sh
#!/bin/bash

# ── Performance setup ──────────────────────────────────────────
sudo nvpmodel -m 0
sudo jetson_clocks
sleep 3

# ── Start Process A (YOLO on local cameras) in background ──────
echo "Starting Process A (YOLO inference)..."
cd /home/user/DeepStream-Yolo/process-a
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt \
  >> /var/log/ds-process-a.log 2>&1 &
PID_A=$!
echo "Process A PID: $PID_A"

# ── Start Process B (relay J1+J2) in background ────────────────
echo "Starting Process B (relay streams)..."
cd /home/user/DeepStream-Yolo/process-b
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt \
  >> /var/log/ds-process-b.log 2>&1 &
PID_B=$!
echo "Process B PID: $PID_B"

# ── Wait for A and B RTSP ports to become available ────────────
echo "Waiting for Process A RTSP (:8556)..."
until gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://127.0.0.1:8556/ds-test" \
  num-buffers=5 ! decodebin ! fakesink > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 5
done
echo "Process A ready!"

echo "Waiting for Process B RTSP (:8557)..."
until gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://127.0.0.1:8557/ds-test" \
  num-buffers=5 ! decodebin ! fakesink > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 5
done
echo "Process B ready!"

# ── Start Process C (combiner: display + website RTSP) ─────────
echo "Starting Process C (display + website RTSP)..."
export DISPLAY=:0
cd /home/user/DeepStream-Yolo/process-c
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt \
  >> /var/log/ds-process-c.log 2>&1 &
PID_C=$!
echo "Process C PID: $PID_C"

echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════"
echo "All processes started."
echo "HDMI display: active"
echo "Website RTSP: rtsp://192.168.1.12:8558/ds-test"
echo "Process A PID: $PID_A  (YOLO cams 9-10)"
echo "Process B PID: $PID_B  (relay cams 1-8)"
echo "Process C PID: $PID_C  (combiner)"
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════"

wait
Make executable and test
chmod +x ~/start_jetson3.sh
~/start_jetson3.sh

# Monitor all 3 processes in real time:
tail -f /var/log/ds-process-a.log /var/log/ds-process-b.log /var/log/ds-process-c.log

Memory & GPU Usage — Will Jetson 3 Handle All 3 Processes?

Concrete numbers so you know exactly what to expect

ProcessGPU Memory (approx)CPU UsageInference Load
Process A ~1.5 GB (YOLO engine + 2 streams) ~20% YOLO FP16 · batch=2 · ~80-120 FPS
Process B ~0.4 GB (decode only, no model) ~8% No inference — just decode + encode
Process C ~0.3 GB (decode + encode + display) ~10% No inference — tile + display + RTSP encode
Total ~2.2 GB of 8 GB ~38% ✅ Well within Orin Nano Super limits
✅
Jetson Orin Nano Super has 8GB unified RAM shared between CPU and GPU. The total estimated usage of ~2.2 GB leaves over 5.5 GB free. Process B and C are extremely lightweight because they have no AI model loaded. You have very comfortable headroom.

The One Rule That Makes This Work

🎯
The entire solution rests on one config line:

In Process B and Process C's config files:
[primary-gie]
enable=0

This single line is what tells DeepStream "skip inference for this entire pipeline." Process A has enable=1 so it runs YOLO normally. Process B and C have enable=0 so they never touch the GPU for inference. Selective inference achieved.

Website Integration URL

Use this URL in your website / dashboard

# For browser dashboard — use MediaMTX relay on Jetson 3:
# ./mediamtx mediamtx.yml
# Then: http://192.168.1.12:8888/all-streams/index.m3u8

# mediamtx.yml config:
paths:
  all-streams:
    source: rtsp://127.0.0.1:8558/ds-test

✅ Selective Inference Confirmed — 3 DeepStream Instances on 1 Jetson

Process A: YOLO on cams 9-10 · Process B: relay J1+J2, enable=0 · Process C: combine, display, RTSP

The key: enable=0 in [primary-gie] = zero inference for that whole process · Each process needs unique rtsp-port and udp-port · Start A → B → C in that order

00 Is It Possible? Direct Answer 01 The Core Problem & What Process B Actually Does 02 Side-by-Side Comparison 03 Method 1 — With Process B (3 Processes) 04 Method 2 — Without Process B (2 Processes) 05 Startup Script — Method 1 06 Startup Script — Method 2 07 Performance & Memory Comparison 08 Which Method Should You Use?

✅ YES — Both Methods Are 100% Possible & Working

Method 1 (with Process B): 3 separate DeepStream processes on Jetson 3. Process A runs YOLO on your 2 local cameras. Process B decodes the J1+J2 RTSP streams and re-encodes them. Process C combines all four and sends to display + RTSP for your website.

Method 2 (without Process B): 2 separate DeepStream processes on Jetson 3. Process A runs YOLO on your 2 local cameras. Process C directly takes the J1+J2 RTSP URLs alongside Process A's output — no middleman. Fewer decode/encode hops, lower latency, less RAM.

Both work. Method 2 is better in every measurable way. Read on for the full reasoning and all configs.

27

The Core Problem & What Process B Actually Does

Understanding exactly what happens to video data in each approach

Why You Need Separate Processes at All

DeepStream's inference plugin (nvinfer) applies to every stream in its pipeline equally. You cannot say "run YOLO on source 0 and 1, skip source 2 and 3" inside one pipeline. The only way to have selective inference is to use separate pipelines (processes). This is not a limitation of Jetson hardware — it is a DeepStream software architecture constraint.

What Process B Does Step by Step

[ WHAT PROCESS B DOES TO THE J1 + J2 STREAMS ]
J1 RTSP :8554
H.264 encoded
already annotated
→
Decode
to raw frames
(GPU decoder)
→
Tile 1×2
(no inference
enable=0)
→
Re-encode
to H.264
(GPU encoder)
→
New RTSP :8557
same video
slightly degraded
J2 RTSP :8554
H.264 encoded
already annotated
↗
❌
The problem with Process B: It takes already-compressed H.264 video, fully decodes it to raw pixels (decode 1), does absolutely nothing useful, then compresses it again (encode 1). This is a generation loss — every encode/decode cycle slightly reduces video quality. It also consumes one GPU decoder slot and one GPU encoder slot for zero benefit. The output of :8557 is slightly worse quality than the input from :8554 and :8554.

What Happens Without Process B

[ WITHOUT PROCESS B — Process C reads J1+J2 DIRECTLY ]
J1 RTSP :8554
annotated H.264
→
Process C
source0
J2 RTSP :8554
annotated H.264
→
Process C
source1
Proc A RTSP :8556
YOLO annotated
→
Process C
source2
Process C
batch=3
enable=0
tile all 3
→
📺 HDMI
sink0
+
📡 RTSP :8558
→ website
sink1

Process C decodes J1, J2, and Process A's output once — to render the tiled display and encode for the website stream. That single decode is unavoidable (you need pixels to display and to encode the combined output). But you save one entire decode+encode round trip that Process B was doing for no reason.

28

Side-by-Side Comparison

Every difference between Method 1 and Method 2

❌ Method 1 — With Process B (3 Processes)

  • 3 DeepStream processes running simultaneously
  • Extra decode+encode for J1+J2 streams in Process B
  • Generation loss — J1+J2 quality degrades slightly
  • Higher latency — J1/J2 streams go through 2 extra codec hops
  • More RAM — Process B holds decoded frame buffers
  • 3 RTSP ports needed — :8556, :8557, :8558
  • More complex startup — 3 processes to manage
  • Works perfectly fine — just not optimal

✅ Method 2 — Without Process B (2 Processes)

  • 2 DeepStream processes — one less to manage
  • No redundant decode/encode for J1+J2 streams
  • Zero generation loss — J1+J2 decoded once, for final output
  • Lower latency — one fewer network hop for J1/J2
  • Less RAM — no extra frame buffers from Process B
  • Only 2 RTSP ports needed — :8556, :8558
  • Simpler — fewer moving parts, easier to debug
  • Better quality output on display and website stream

bitrate=6000000   # 6 Mbps for combined 3-zone output
enc-type=0   # Hardware encoder
rtsp-port=8558   # Access: rtsp://192.168.1.12:8558/ds-test
udp-port=5404
✅
Method 2 needs NO config_infer file for Process C — because enable=0. Only Process A needs a config_infer file. That's one less file to maintain.
31

Startup Script — Method 1 (3 Processes)

Start all three processes in the correct order with readiness checks

~/start_method1.sh
#!/bin/bash
set -e
BASE=~/DeepStream-Yolo
LOG=/var/log/deepstream
mkdir -p $LOG

echo "═══ Jetson 3 — Method 1 (3 processes) ═══"
sudo nvpmodel -m 0 && sudo jetson_clocks
sleep 3

# ── 1. Start Process A (YOLO on cams 9-10) ──────────────────
echo "[1/3] Starting Process A — YOLO inference..."
cd $BASE/process-a
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt >> $LOG/proc-a.log 2>&1 &
PID_A=$!

# Wait for Process A RTSP to be ready
echo "Waiting for Process A to start streaming on :8556..."
until gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://127.0.0.1:8556/ds-test" \
  num-buffers=3 ! decodebin ! fakesink > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 8
done
echo "✓ Process A ready (PID: $PID_A)"

# ── 2. Start Process B (relay J1+J2, no inference) ──────────
echo "[2/3] Starting Process B — relay J1+J2..."
cd $BASE/process-b
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt >> $LOG/proc-b.log 2>&1 &
PID_B=$!

echo "Waiting for Process B to start streaming on :8557..."
until gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://127.0.0.1:8557/ds-test" \
  num-buffers=3 ! decodebin ! fakesink > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 5
done
echo "✓ Process B ready (PID: $PID_B)"

# ── 3. Start Process C (combiner: display + website RTSP) ────
echo "[3/3] Starting Process C — display + website RTSP..."
export DISPLAY=:0
cd $BASE/process-c
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt >> $LOG/proc-c.log 2>&1 &
PID_C=$!

echo ""
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════"
echo "✅ All 3 processes running."
echo "   HDMI display : active (Jetson 3 HDMI port)"
echo "   Website RTSP : rtsp://192.168.1.12:8558/ds-test"
echo "   Process A PID: $PID_A  — logs: $LOG/proc-a.log"
echo "   Process B PID: $PID_B  — logs: $LOG/proc-b.log"
echo "   Process C PID: $PID_C  — logs: $LOG/proc-c.log"
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════"

wait

Startup Script — Method 2 (2 Processes, Recommended)

Simpler script, fewer processes, same result

~/start_method2.sh ← USE THIS ONE
#!/bin/bash
set -e
BASE=~/DeepStream-Yolo
LOG=/var/log/deepstream
mkdir -p $LOG

echo "═══ Jetson 3 — Method 2 (2 processes, optimised) ═══"
sudo nvpmodel -m 0 && sudo jetson_clocks
sleep 3

# ── Verify upstream Jetsons are reachable ────────────────────
echo "Checking Jetson 1 RTSP (:8554)..."
until gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://192.168.1.10:8554/ds-test" \
  num-buffers=3 ! decodebin ! fakesink > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  echo "  J1 not ready, retrying in 10s..."
  sleep 10
done
echo "✓ Jetson 1 reachable"

echo "Checking Jetson 2 RTSP (:8554)..."
until gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://192.168.1.11:8554/ds-test" \
  num-buffers=3 ! decodebin ! fakesink > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  echo "  J2 not ready, retrying in 10s..."
  sleep 10
done
echo "✓ Jetson 2 reachable"

# ── 1. Start Process A (YOLO on cams 9-10) ──────────────────
echo "[1/2] Starting Process A — YOLO on cameras 9 & 10..."
cd $BASE/process-a
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt >> $LOG/proc-a.log 2>&1 &
PID_A=$!

echo "Waiting for Process A RTSP on :8556..."
until gst-launch-1.0 rtspsrc location="rtsp://127.0.0.1:8556/ds-test" \
  num-buffers=3 ! decodebin ! fakesink > /dev/null 2>&1; do
  sleep 8
done
echo "✓ Process A ready (PID: $PID_A)"

# ── 2. Start Process C (3-source combiner) ───────────────────
echo "[2/2] Starting Process C — combine J1+J2+A → display + website RTSP..."
export DISPLAY=:0
cd $BASE/process-c
deepstream-app -c deepstream_app_config.txt >> $LOG/proc-c.log 2>&1 &
PID_C=$!

echo ""
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════"
echo "✅ Method 2 running. 2 processes total."
echo "   HDMI display  : active (1×3 grid — all 10 cams)"
echo "   Website RTSP  : rtsp://192.168.1.12:8558/ds-test"
echo "   Process A PID : $PID_A  — logs: $LOG/proc-a.log"
echo "   Process C PID : $PID_C  — logs: $LOG/proc-c.log"
echo "═══════════════════════════════════════════════"

wait
Make executable and run
chmod +x ~/start_method2.sh
~/start_method2.sh

# Monitor live logs:
tail -f /var/log/deepstream/proc-a.log /var/log/deepstream/proc-c.log

# Test website RTSP from another machine:
vlc rtsp://192.168.1.12:8558/ds-test

Performance & Memory Comparison

Concrete numbers for both methods on Jetson Orin Nano Super (8GB)

Component Method 1 (with Process B) Method 2 (without Process B) Winner
Active processes 3 (A + B + C) 2 (A + C) Method 2
GPU decoders used 4 (A×2 + B×2 + C×2) 4 (A×2 + C×3) Same
GPU encoders used 3 (A×1 + B×1 + C×1) 2 (A×1 + C×1) Method 2
RAM estimate ~2.5 GB ~2.0 GB Method 2
J1/J2 decode/encode hops 2× (B + C) 1× (C only) Method 2
J1/J2 output quality Slight loss (re-encoded by B) No quality loss Method 2
End-to-end latency Higher (~50-100ms extra from B) Lower Method 2
Config files to maintain 3 deepstream configs + 1 infer config 2 deepstream configs + 1 infer config Method 2
Complexity More complex Simpler Method 2
Does it work? ✅ Yes ✅ Yes Both work
✅
Both methods fit comfortably in the Orin Nano Super's 8GB. The YOLO model (Process A) uses ~1.5 GB. Everything else is decode/encode buffers. Method 1 uses ~2.5 GB total, Method 2 uses ~2.0 GB total. Either way you have 5-6 GB of headroom remaining.
34

Which Method Should You Use?

The definitive answer with one scenario where Method 1 makes sense

Use Method 1 only if…

  • You need Process B's output as a standalone recording (e.g. recording just J1+J2 combined to a file)
  • You want to add a second GIE on just the relay streams (e.g. secondary analytics on J1/J2 zone only)
  • Your network to J1/J2 is unreliable and you want Process B to buffer and absorb jitter before Process C sees it
  • Otherwise: there is no advantage to Method 1.

Use Method 2 in all other cases

  • Fewer processes = easier to manage and debug
  • No quality degradation on J1/J2 streams
  • Lower latency end-to-end
  • Less RAM and GPU encoder usage
  • The startup script is shorter and cleaner
  • Process C with batch=3 and enable=0 is very lightweight
  • This is the production-ready choice.

The One Rule That Stays the Same in Both Methods

🎯
Selective inference is achieved by using separate DeepStream processes, not by filtering within one process.

Process A: [primary-gie] enable=1 → YOLO runs on cams 9 and 10.
Process C: [primary-gie] enable=0 → zero inference, just tile and output.

This is the only correct way to do selective inference in DeepStream. Both methods use this principle. Method 2 just removes the unnecessary middleman (Process B) that was between J1/J2 and Process C.
